query: returning to the burned family hall and finding the compass on the hearthstone

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
It smelled of rain — wet stone, leaf rot, and the faint ghost of old smoke.
Eleanor stopped a few paces short of the gate. It had been ten years.
The hall was smaller than she remembered; in her memory it had been a great dark house ringed by old elms, but what stood in front of her now was a half-collapsed shell of the east wing and one wing that had somehow kept its roof.
"A ruin," she said.
She had not meant to say it to anyone. It simply came out.
The door to the keeping-room was not locked. There had been a lock, but it had fallen, hasp and all. Eleanor picked it up, turned it over for a while, and set it back where it had lain. It was no use now.
Inside, the floorboards spoke. One at every step.
Something had been left on the old hearthstone.
A compass.
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

candidates.sceneTitle: Interlude: The Hearthstone
candidates.chunkText:
The moon was up. Eleanor went back to the keeping-room once more.
Beside the hearth, in a place she had not noticed the first time, something lay. She crouched and picked it up — the remains of an old token, a thread of faded Ashveil vermilion still on its face.
It was the token her mother had tied to the hearth ten years ago, knotted before the fire, and no one should have touched it since.
Holding the token, she turned toward the door. The hand that knocked the lock from its hasp had untied this, too.
Someone has been coming to the hall. Ever since the fire, all this time.

candidates.sceneTitle: Bonus: The Origin of the Compass (complete)
candidates.chunkText:
The compass was not made; it was bound. The first of the Ashveil line carried a needle of cold iron to the King's Fountain and gave it a single drop of blood, and from that night the needle pointed not to north but to kin.
Every heir since has fed it the same way. The needle remembers each hand that held it. That is why, ten years untended on the hearthstone, it was still warm — it had not forgotten Eleanor.

candidates.sceneTitle: Part Three, Scene 1: at Ironhaven
candidates.chunkText:
The floor of the keeping-room had not rotted. Someone had been tending it. For ten years untouched, it was unnaturally whole.
Brother Anselm drew out the compass from inside their coat. The vermilion on its face had worn thin, but it still held a faint warmth in Brother Anselm's hand.
Beside the hearth hung a paper token Brother Anselm did not remember. The ink was still fresh. It had been written yesterday, or the day before at most.
Brother Anselm reached toward the token, then stopped. To touch it was to be certain. To be certain was to be unable to turn back.
'Can I trust Old Edran?' Brother Anselm asked themselves. No answer came yet. Perhaps it was better that none did.
'Mira is coming,' someone said. Brother Anselm could not tell whose voice it was — not Old Edran's, not their own, but a voice from somewhere far.
Brother Anselm nodded without a word. That was the whole of the answer. It was enough.

candidates.sceneTitle: Part Three, Scene 1: at Ironhaven
candidates.chunkText:
Brother Anselm returned the compass to their coat. The time to use it might come. Hoping it would not, they kept it ready all the same.
'You had the compass all this time,' Old Edran murmured, surprised. 'Then this is simple. Let us finish what we started ten years ago.'
Brother Anselm reached toward the token, then stopped. To touch it was to be certain. To be certain was to be unable to turn back.
The road back to Ironhaven was the same one they had come by, yet it felt longer. The hills stood sharper than memory, and the river ran loud.
Brother Anselm took a firmer hold of the compass. Their fingertips were cold. Within the cold, a small warmth remained.
An old burn scar still marked Brother Anselm's wrist. It had been made on the night ten years past. The pain should have gone long ago, yet on wet days it ached.
'Do you remember now?' Old Edran asked. Brother Anselm did not answer. There are things in the world one would rather not remember.

candidates.sceneTitle: Memory: The Night of the Fire
candidates.chunkText:
[Memory: ten years ago, summer]
The house was burning.
Eleanor had stood before the keeping-room. She still did not understand what had happened. The fire wrapped the east wing, caught the elms, and stained the night hills red.
"Get back," a voice said. Whose voice it was, Eleanor still cannot say.
She ran. The compass in her hand, she simply ran.
When she looked back, the roof of the east wing came down.
What had been inside the house that night — she saw it. She must have seen it. But now only the colour of the fire, the heat, and someone's shout remain.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.
She reached out slowly. The compass was dry. It had been left to ten years of rain, and it was not wet.
The moment her finger touched it, the memory came.
It was not her own memory.
She let out a breath and drew back her hand. As she took the compass up again, the seal pressed into its case sat differently than before, or so it seemed.
When she looked closely, the mark was doubled, and she could not tell which was the true Ashveil seal.
Wind moved, and under the eaves an iron weathervane that had not been there ten years ago turned and gave a small, thin cry.

A compass.

candidates.sceneTitle: Memory: The Night of the Fire
candidates.chunkText:
[Memory: ten years ago, summer]
The house was burning.
Eleanor had stood before the keeping-room. She still did not understand what had happened. The fire wrapped the east wing, caught the elms, and stained the night hills red.
"Get back," a voice said. Whose voice it was, Eleanor still cannot say.
She ran. The compass in her hand, she simply ran.
When she looked back, the roof of the east wing came down.
What had been inside the house that night — she saw it. She must have seen it. But now only the colour of the fire, the heat, and someone's shout remain.

What her mother spoke that night was not a spell but a litany — the names of the bound, said in order, so that none would be forgotten in the dark.
Eleanor remembers the cadence and not the words. The fire took the words. The cadence is all that survived, and on bad nights she catches herself keeping its time.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter Two: The Writ
candidates.chunkText:
When Eleanor woke, the compass was in her hand. Through the gaps of her clenched fingers it gave off a dry warmth.
Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.
The door opened without a knock. Wrenna stood there as if ten years were nothing. 'So you came after all,' she said, and held out a small wrapped parcel.
Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

[Memory: ten years ago, summer]
The house was burning.
Eleanor had stood before the keeping-room. She still did not understand what had happened. The fire wrapped the east wing, caught the elms, and stained the night hills red.
"Get back," a voice said. Whose voice it was, Eleanor still cannot say.
She ran. The compass in her hand, she simply ran.
When she looked back, the roof of the east wing came down.
What had been inside the house that night — she saw it. She must have seen it. But now only the colour of the fire, the heat, and someone's shout remain.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.
She reached out slowly. The compass was dry. It had been left to ten years of rain, and it was not wet.
The moment her finger touched it, the memory came.
It was not her own memory.
She let out a breath and drew back her hand. As she took the compass up again, the seal pressed into its case sat differently than before, or so it seemed.
When she looked closely, the mark was doubled, and she could not tell which was the true Ashveil seal.
Wind moved, and under the eaves an iron weathervane that had not been there ten years ago turned and gave a small, thin cry.

candidates.chunkText:
It smelled of rain — wet stone, leaf rot, and the faint ghost of old smoke.
Eleanor stopped a few paces short of the gate. It had been ten years.
The hall was smaller than she remembered; in her memory it had been a great dark house ringed by old elms, but what stood in front of her now was a half-collapsed shell of the east wing and one wing that had somehow kept its roof.
"A ruin," she said.
She had not meant to say it to anyone. It simply came out.
The door to the keeping-room was not locked. There had been a lock, but it had fallen, hasp and all. Eleanor picked it up, turned it over for a while, and set it back where it had lain. It was no use now.
Inside, the floorboards spoke. One at every step.
Something had been left on the old hearthstone.
A compass.
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

Someone has been coming to the hall. Ever since the fire, all this time.

candidates.chunkText:
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.
She reached out slowly. The compass was dry. It had been left to ten years of rain, and it was not wet.
The moment her finger touched it, the memory came.
It was not her own memory.
She let out a breath and drew back her hand. As she took the compass up again, the seal pressed into its case sat differently than before, or so it seemed.
When she looked closely, the mark was doubled, and she could not tell which was the true Ashveil seal.
Wind moved, and under the eaves an iron weathervane that had not been there ten years ago turned and gave a small, thin cry.

candidates.sceneTitle: Bonus: The Origin of the Compass (complete)
candidates.chunkText:
The compass was not made; it was bound. The first of the Ashveil line carried a needle of cold iron to the King's Fountain and gave it a single drop of blood, and from that night the needle pointed not to north but to kin.
Every heir since has fed it the same way. The needle remembers each hand that held it. That is why, ten years untended on the hearthstone, it was still warm — it had not forgotten Eleanor.

Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.

Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

'I have to find Aldric,' Gerard Thorne thought. But there was something to be sure of first.

The door groaned. Gerard Thorne's hand went to the compass on reflex. But it was Aldric who stepped in. 'Did I startle you,' Aldric said shortly.
The sky over The Guard Hall was the colour of slate. Clouds hung low, and far off there was thunder. Less than an hour before the rain.
'Do you remember now?' Aldric asked. Gerard Thorne did not answer. There are things in the world one would rather not remember.

candidates.sceneTitle: Part Three, Scene 7: at The Guard Hall
candidates.chunkText:
'There is no record of Mira here,' Aldric said. 'Someone removed it. Recently, too.'
Gerard Thorne took a long breath. Counting to three, they let it out slowly. They did it four times, until the pulse went quiet.
Gerard Thorne stopped before the old shelves. The spines were rubbed smooth, half of them unreadable. Even so, one book caught Gerard Thorne's eye.

Saying the name of Mira aloud was still hard. It was a name that answered when it was called.
Night deepened. Every light in The Guard Hall was out, and there was nothing to hear but the wind and Gerard Thorne's own heartbeat.
Gerard Thorne nodded without a word. That was the whole of the answer. It was enough.

Back in Ironhaven, Eleanor meets the Citadel knight Aldric.
Purpose: introduce Aldric. Plain-looking and courteous on the surface, but something is off — the face of a man who knows a thing and is not saying it.
Aldric already knows that Eleanor has travelled to Greymoor and back — to the ruined hall. That she went home at all is something he should not know. That becomes a planted hook.
To decide: does Aldric approach Eleanor, or does Eleanor seek out Aldric? Which one moves first changes the first read on the balance of power between them.

It smelled of rain — wet stone, leaf rot, and the faint ghost of old smoke.
Eleanor stopped a few paces short of the gate. It had been ten years.
The hall was smaller than she remembered; in her memory it had been a great dark house ringed by old elms, but what stood in front of her now was a half-collapsed shell of the east wing and one wing that had somehow kept its roof.
"A ruin," she said.
She had not meant to say it to anyone. It simply came out.
The door to the keeping-room was not locked. There had been a lock, but it had fallen, hasp and all. Eleanor picked it up, turned it over for a while, and set it back where it had lain. It was no use now.
Inside, the floorboards spoke. One at every step.
Something had been left on the old hearthstone.
A compass.
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

candidates.sceneTitle: Part Five, Scene 7: at The Sealed Vault
candidates.chunkText:
'I have to find Aldric,' Brother Anselm thought. But there was something to be sure of first.
Brother Anselm took a firmer hold of The Rite Copybook. Their fingertips were cold. Within the cold, a small warmth remained.
Much had changed since then, but the look of this place had barely moved. The elms of The Sealed Vault had grown tall, cutting the sky into narrow strips.
There was no one at The Sealed Vault. By this hour the morning market should have been open, but there were no stalls and no buyers. Only the cold air drifted.
Brother Anselm drew out The Rite Copybook from inside their coat. The vermilion on its face had worn thin, but it still held a faint warmth in Brother Anselm's hand.
'Mira is coming,' someone said. Brother Anselm could not tell whose voice it was — not Aldric's, not their own, but a voice from somewhere far.
'Mira is real,' Aldric said quietly. 'Whether you believe it or not.'

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.
She reached out slowly. The compass was dry. It had been left to ten years of rain, and it was not wet.
The moment her finger touched it, the memory came.
It was not her own memory.
She let out a breath and drew back her hand. As she took the compass up again, the seal pressed into its case sat differently than before, or so it seemed.
When she looked closely, the mark was doubled, and she could not tell which was the true Ashveil seal.
Wind moved, and under the eaves an iron weathervane that had not been there ten years ago turned and gave a small, thin cry.

'You came,' said a voice from behind. Silas turned. Cassian Vale was standing there. Why, Silas did not ask. It seemed better not to.
'Mira is real,' Cassian Vale said quietly. 'Whether you believe it or not.'
Saying the name of Mira aloud was still hard. It was a name that answered when it was called.
Silas took a firmer hold of Hallow Salt. Their fingertips were cold. Within the cold, a small warmth remained.
'Do not touch Ashveil Hall,' Cassian Vale said sharply. 'The ward still holds there. Move it carelessly and the whole thing comes down.'
Silas took a long breath. Counting to three, they let it out slowly. They did it four times, until the pulse went quiet.
Rain began to fall. At first it was too thin to notice. Then it wet Silas's hair and darkened the vermilion of Hallow Salt by a shade.
Silas returned Hallow Salt to their coat. The time to use it might come. Hoping it would not, they kept it ready all the same.

candidates.sceneTitle: Bonus: The Origin of the Compass (complete)

The compass was not made; it was bound. The first of the Ashveil line carried a needle of cold iron to the King's Fountain and gave it a single drop of blood, and from that night the needle pointed not to north but to kin.

candidates.sceneTitle: Memory: The Night of the Fire
candidates.chunkText:
[Memory: ten years ago, summer]
The house was burning.
Eleanor had stood before the keeping-room. She still did not understand what had happened. The fire wrapped the east wing, caught the elms, and stained the night hills red.
"Get back," a voice said. Whose voice it was, Eleanor still cannot say.
She ran. The compass in her hand, she simply ran.
When she looked back, the roof of the east wing came down.
What had been inside the house that night — she saw it. She must have seen it. But now only the colour of the fire, the heat, and someone's shout remain.

candidates.sceneTitle: Bonus: The Litany of the Burning Night (final)
candidates.chunkText:
What her mother spoke that night was not a spell but a litany — the names of the bound, said in order, so that none would be forgotten in the dark.
Eleanor remembers the cadence and not the words. The fire took the words. The cadence is all that survived, and on bad nights she catches herself keeping its time.

Beside the hearth, in a place she had not noticed the first time, something lay. She crouched and picked it up — the remains of an old token, a thread of faded Ashveil vermilion still on its face.
It was the token her mother had tied to the hearth ten years ago, knotted before the fire, and no one should have touched it since.
Holding the token, she turned toward the door. The hand that knocked the lock from its hasp had untied this, too.
Someone has been coming to the hall. Ever since the fire, all this time.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter Two: The Writ
candidates.chunkText:
When Eleanor woke, the compass was in her hand. Through the gaps of her clenched fingers it gave off a dry warmth.
Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.
The door opened without a knock. Wrenna stood there as if ten years were nothing. 'So you came after all,' she said, and held out a small wrapped parcel.
Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

Tamsin reached toward the token, then stopped. To touch it was to be certain. To be certain was to be unable to turn back.
Night deepened. Every light in Silas's Apothecary was out, and there was nothing to hear but the wind and Tamsin's own heartbeat.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter Two: The Writ
candidates.chunkText:
When Eleanor woke, the compass was in her hand. Through the gaps of her clenched fingers it gave off a dry warmth.
Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.
The door opened without a knock. Wrenna stood there as if ten years were nothing. 'So you came after all,' she said, and held out a small wrapped parcel.
Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter Three: Ironhaven by Night
candidates.chunkText:
[OUTLINE - to be written]
Back in Ironhaven, Eleanor meets the Citadel knight Aldric.
Purpose: introduce Aldric. Plain-looking and courteous on the surface, but something is off — the face of a man who knows a thing and is not saying it.
Aldric already knows that Eleanor has travelled to Greymoor and back — to the ruined hall. That she went home at all is something he should not know. That becomes a planted hook.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
It smelled of rain — wet stone, leaf rot, and the faint ghost of old smoke.
Eleanor stopped a few paces short of the gate. It had been ten years.
The hall was smaller than she remembered; in her memory it had been a great dark house ringed by old elms, but what stood in front of her now was a half-collapsed shell of the east wing and one wing that had somehow kept its roof.
"A ruin," she said.
She had not meant to say it to anyone. It simply came out.
The door to the keeping-room was not locked. There had been a lock, but it had fallen, hasp and all. Eleanor picked it up, turned it over for a while, and set it back where it had lain. It was no use now.
Inside, the floorboards spoke. One at every step.
Something had been left on the old hearthstone.
A compass.
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.
The door opened without a knock. Wrenna stood there as if ten years were nothing. 'So you came after all,' she said, and held out a small wrapped parcel.
Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

candidates.sceneTitle: Chapter One: The Hall
candidates.chunkText:
It smelled of rain — wet stone, leaf rot, and the faint ghost of old smoke.
Eleanor stopped a few paces short of the gate. It had been ten years.
The hall was smaller than she remembered; in her memory it had been a great dark house ringed by old elms, but what stood in front of her now was a half-collapsed shell of the east wing and one wing that had somehow kept its roof.
"A ruin," she said.
She had not meant to say it to anyone. It simply came out.
The door to the keeping-room was not locked. There had been a lock, but it had fallen, hasp and all. Eleanor picked it up, turned it over for a while, and set it back where it had lain. It was no use now.
Inside, the floorboards spoke. One at every step.
Something had been left on the old hearthstone.
A compass.
Eleanor could not move. When she had left this place ten years ago, she had set the compass on the hearth and walked away. Someone had not taken it — they had left it here, all this time. Or it had come back.

The compass was not made; it was bound. The first of the Ashveil line carried a needle of cold iron to the King's Fountain and gave it a single drop of blood, and from that night the needle pointed not to north but to kin.

When Eleanor woke, the compass was in her hand. Through the gaps of her clenched fingers it gave off a dry warmth.
Someone was running. Someone was afraid. Who, she could not fix. Only the outline of the memory stayed; the inside was thin.
Under the compass lay a writ, sealed and uncreased by ten years. Her own name stood at the top. Below it, in two words, Come back, and beneath that the steps of the Sundering Rite.
The final line she could not read. It was not blacked out; her eye simply slid off it, the way a hand slides off wet glass.
The door opened without a knock. Wrenna stood there as if ten years were nothing. 'So you came after all,' she said, and held out a small wrapped parcel.
Eleanor did not ask how Wrenna had known she would come. She found that she could not.

[Memory: ten years ago, summer]
The house was burning.
Eleanor had stood before the keeping-room. She still did not understand what had happened. The fire wrapped the east wing, caught the elms, and stained the night hills red.

The compass was not made; it was bound. The first of the Ashveil line carried a needle of cold iron to the King's Fountain and gave it a single drop of blood, and from that night the needle pointed not to north but to kin.
